explanations.positive_explanation: This neuron lights up on tokens that start or belong to headings/titles—e.g. article or section titles, email subjects, Q/A questions, blog post titles, news‐style headlines—marking the text’s structural “header.”
explanations.negative_explanation:
Here’s a concise interpretation for each feature based on its highest‐activation tokens and contexts:

• Feature “z”  
  Detects the initial “z” in lowercase words or usernames (e.g. zangobot, zombiegoddess666).  

• Feature “PE”  
  Flags the uppercase prefix “PE” in acronyms or titles (e.g. PEKK, PEAKY BLINDERS).  

• Feature “Compar”  
  Catches the “Compar” prefix of the word “Comparison” in scientific‐paper contexts.  

• Feature “ec”  
  Marks the “ec” fragment in the domain name ecoi.net (a refugee‐information portal).  

• Feature “version”  
  Identifies the key “version” in config or Dockerfile metadata (e.g. version: "3.7").  

• Feature “et”  
  Picks out the subword “et” (the tail of “Let”) in formal math‐problem statements.  

• Feature “pe”  
  Highlights the lowercase “pe” prefix in ordinary nouns (e.g. peasant).  

• Feature “Cap”  
  Flags the uppercase “Cap” prefix in proper names (e.g. Capilano University, Capitanich).  

• Feature “environment”  
  Captures the full word “environment(al)” in news‐style writing (e.g. environmental defenders).  

• Feature “te”  
  Detects the subword “te” (from “the,” “least,” “greatest,” etc.) in math‐English.  

• Feature “BI”  
  Targets the “BI” prefix in the acronym BIM (Building Information Modeling).  

• Feature “pl”  
  Catches the “pl” prefix in technical nouns like “plastic.”  

• Feature “GM”  
  Flags the uppercase acronym “GM” in corporate headlines (e.g. GM → Government Motors).

explanations.positive_explanation: This neuron detects the word “such” (especially in the phrase “such as”) when it’s used to introduce examples or illustrative comparisons.
explanations.negative_explanation: This neuron fires on tokens that occur in top‐level headings or titles—e.g. the leading year of a Wikipedia article, words like “Report,” “Analysis,” “Blog,” “version,” “Office,” or domain fragments (“com”) in header metadata. In other words, it detects section‐/page‐heading tokens at the start of documents.
